claims.text: Dallas started using 50 AI-powered cameras on bulky sanitation trucks in mid-April 2026 to scan for overgrown lawns, debris, unsafe structures, graffiti and sidewalk issues.
claims.quote: The city started using 50 AI-powered cameras mounted on bulky sanitation trucks in mid-April to scan for possible property and right-of-way concerns, including overgrown lawns, debris, unsafe structures, graffiti and sidewalk issues.

claims.text: The vendor is City Detect, whose computer vision software scans the images in a U.S. cloud system.
claims.quote: The images are sent to a cloud-based system in the U.S., where the company City Detect’s computer vision software scans for potential concerns.

claims.text: The cameras take still photos along regular sanitation routes and do not record continuous video.
claims.quote: The cameras take still photos as the trucks travel their regular sanitation routes. They don’t record continuous video.

claims.text: The three-year camera contract is an estimated $2,556,000, subject to annual council appropriations.
claims.quote: The three-year AI camera contract is an estimated $2,556,000, subject to annual City Council appropriations.

claims.text: In about four months the cameras photographed more than 20,000 code concerns.
claims.quote: In just four months, the cameras have photographed more than 20,000 code concerns.

claims.text: As of the October 2026 committee briefing, staff had reviewed 5,318 observations, sent 2,928 courtesy notices and conducted 473 field inspections.
claims.quote: Staff have reviewed 5,318 observations, sent 2,928 courtesy notices and conducted 473 field inspections.

claims.text: As of the same briefing, the department reported 374 voluntary corrections and 101 formal enforcement actions.
claims.quote: The department also reported 374 voluntary corrections and 101 formal enforcement actions.

claims.text: A September 8th, 2026 city memo said the cameras had scanned 10,000 properties, producing 3,700 violations with notices and 57 citations at 34 properties.
claims.quote: According to the memo, the cameras have scanned 10,000 properties and have resulted in 3,700 violations, resulting in notices from the city. 57 citations have also been handed out at 34 properties from what the cameras have scanned.

claims.text: Faces and license plates are blurred and images are kept for 12 months.
claims.quote: Faces and license plates are blurred, and images are retained for 12 months under city records-retention requirements.

claims.text: A citation comes only after a code officer inspects in person, notifies the owner and the condition stays unresolved.
claims.quote: Citations are issued only after a code officer inspects the property, provides notice to the owner and the condition remains unresolved.

claims.text: Revised notices will carry a QR code to the city's Housing and Community Empowerment resource page, and council members asked for Spanish versions.
claims.quote: The notices will also have a QR code linking residents to the city’s Housing and Community Empowerment resource page and provide additional contacts for residents with questions. Council members also asked that notices be available in Spanish.

claims.text: After NBC 5 questioned a photo with an unblurred plate, Dallas asked City Detect to run all photos through blurring again.
claims.quote: Reed said after NBC 5 Investigates questioned the photo, his team sent it back to City Detect and asked the company to run all photos in the system through the blurring process.

claims.text: Assistant director Jeremy Reed said code compliance has no need or desire to see faces and plates.
claims.quote: I would say code compliance has no need or desire to see faces and license plates. That's why we've asked for the blurring to happen,

claims.text: Director Chris Christian said the cameras run along existing citywide sanitation routes and are not intended to target communities by income or demographics.
claims.quote: Code Compliance Director Chris Christian said the cameras operate along existing sanitation routes throughout the city and are not intended to target communities based on income or demographics.

claims.text: City heat maps show the cameras documented more issues in southern Dallas, raising questions about added scrutiny on neighborhoods with fewer resources for repairs.
claims.quote: Heat maps provided by the city's code compliance department show the AI cameras documented more issues in southern Dallas. The maps raise questions about whether the system could place more scrutiny on neighborhoods with older homes, more deferred maintenance or fewer resources for repairs.

claims.text: City officials said only code compliance and sanitation employees can access the software and its images.
claims.quote: City officials said only code compliance and sanitation employees have access to the software and the images it collects.

claims.text: City records showed more than 21,000 properties with at least one possible violation, each given a blight score from 1 to 4.
claims.quote: Artificial intelligence identified at least one possible code violation on more than 21,000 properties, according to the records. Those properties were then assigned a "blight score" from 1 to 4, ranging from least severe to most severe.

claims.text: The system assigns images an index to help city staff prioritize which ones to review first.
claims.quote: The system also assigns images an index to help city staff prioritize which ones to review first.

claims.text: The most common observations were lawn debris, grass height, vehicles on lawns, weeds, litter and peeling or damaged exterior surfaces.
claims.quote: The most common observations included lawn debris, grass height, vehicles on lawns, weeds, litter and peeling or damaged exterior surfaces.

claims.text: For a flagged image staff can take no action, monitor, send a courtesy notice, request an inspection or refer it to a city crew.
claims.quote: They can take no action, monitor the condition, send a courtesy notice, create a service request for an inspection or refer an eligible problem to a city crew for abatement.

claims.text: A courtesy notice does not open an enforcement case or set a formal deadline.
claims.quote: The city says a courtesy notice does not open an enforcement case or set a formal deadline to fix the issue.

claims.text: One city-released photo carried a black box reading motor vehicle over a plate.
claims.quote: one photo had a large black box over the license plate with the words “motor vehicle” written on it.

claims.text: The vendor told the city its blurring is about 99 percent effective.
claims.quote: they told us that generally the effectiveness of that process is about 99% effective.

claims.text: Photos are stamped with the date and time at an address, and vehicle markings can show even when plates are blurred.
claims.quote: Unique vehicle markings such as bumper stickers or paint designs can be seen, and the photos are stamped with the date and time they were taken at a particular address.

claims.text: One property got a blight score of 2 for a chimney paint issue.
claims.quote: City records obtained by NBC 5 showed that a trash truck camera detected a "chimney paint" issue and assigned the property a blight score of 2.

claims.text: Before launch, the only measurable goal was 5,200 courtesy notices a year after full rollout.
claims.quote: "Before implementation, the only measurable goal was the issuance of 5,200 courtesy notices per year following full rollout."

claims.text: About 13,800 of the 20,000 photographed concerns came from southern Dallas.
claims.quote: Properties in southern Dallas also made up a majority of the photographed concerns, at about 13,800 of the 20,000 images, according to a Dallas Morning News analysis of city data. The highest concentration was in the 75216 ZIP code and Cedar Crest neighborhood.

claims.text: Less than 2 percent of southern Dallas flags became courtesy notices, against more than 4 percent elsewhere.
claims.quote: Less than 2% of flagged observations in southern Dallas resulted in a courtesy notice. In the rest of the city, which collected about 7,300 code concerns, more than 4% of observations resulted in courtesy notices.

claims.text: Side-mounted cameras periodically photograph the curb line visible from the public right-of-way as brush trucks run their routes.
claims.quote: As brush trucks run their normal routes, side-mounted cameras will periodically take still photos of the curb line visible from the public right-of-way.

claims.text: City Detect's CEO told the committee the blurring was expanded to cover a person's full image.
claims.quote: City Detect CEO Gavin Baum-Blake told the committee that the company had expanded its blurring technology to cover a person’s full image.

claims.text: Christian said camera observations and resident service requests correlate almost exactly on the maps.
claims.quote: He pointed to maps comparing camera observations with code compliance service requests, saying the patterns “correlate almost exactly.”

claims.text: City Detect says its system has no plate database or plate search.
claims.quote: There is no plate database, no plate index, and no connection to any external plate or law enforcement database.

claims.text: City officials said about 80 percent of owners fix the concern after a notice with no further city action.
claims.quote: City officials say approximately 80% of property owners address the reported concern after receiving a notice, without requiring further action from the city.
